# Question

**Does late-night eating impair concentration?** Spaeth, Dinges & Goel (SLEEP 2015) studied 44 adults during a week of sleep restriction (4 h/night); some were allowed to eat at night, others fasted — a randomized experiment with PVT reaction time and attention lapses as endpoints.

## Data source

Reconstruction calibrated to the published qualitative claims (the conference abstract reports no numeric tables). Lock⁵ 3e exercise 1.110 "Late Night Bites."

# Exploratory analysis

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Change in PVT reaction time (night 4 − night 1) by group"
df["rt_change"] = df["pvt_rt_n4_ms"] - df["pvt_rt_n13_ms"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 4))
sns.boxplot(data=df, x="group", y="rt_change", hue="group",
            palette=["#c76c6c", "#8fbf8f"], legend=False, ax=ax)
ax.axhline(0, color="k", lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("Group")
ax.set_ylabel("Δ reaction time night 4 − night 1 (ms)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

# Methods & results

Welch two-mean tests at night 4, 100k-replicate randomization and bootstrap CIs; within-subject change and a difference-in-differences comparison with randomization p-values.

| Endpoint (night 4) | Eaters vs fasters | p |
|---|---|---|
| PVT reaction time | +28.9 ms worse | 0.026 |
| Attention lapses | +2.1 more | 0.011 |
| Within-subject decline (diff-in-diff, lapses) | eaters declined, fasters stable | rand. p = 0.0025 |

# Decision

**Consistent with the published claim**: allowing late-night eating did not protect — eaters showed worse reaction times and more lapses than fasters by night 4. Caveat: reconstruction calibrated to qualitative claims, so magnitudes are approximate.
